query: For high-entropy alloys in demanding engineering applications, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, defines the conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment that could falsify it?

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a stable and coherent L1_2 γ′ precipitate phase in high-entropy alloys can improve resistance to thermally induced toughness loss by providing a mechanism for precipitation strengthening and stabilizing the microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a face-centered cubic (FCC) matrix
generation.intervention: Introduction of a stable and coherent L1_2 γ′ precipitate phase
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening and microstructural stabilization, as derived from materials-science principles and supported by records judged as transfers or partially, such as PMC10759803::chunk::001::introduction::0f933d56a0
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, as evidenced by increased yield strength and creep resistance
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy without the introduction of a stable and coherent L1_2 γ′ precipitate phase
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and processing conditions required to achieve the desired microstructure and properties are still uncertain and require further research

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile and creep tests on high-entropy alloys with and without the introduction of a stable and coherent L1_2 γ′ precipitate phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of a stable and coherent L1_2 γ′ precipitate phase does not result in improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text:
In the last few decades, the development of nickel-based superalloys has allowed a steady increase in operating temperatures of jet turbine engines, which leads to enhanced engine performance and efficiency. However, nowadays the engine operating temperatures have reached around 80% of the melting points of the materials, [1] i.e. , almost reaching the upper limit of usability, making it impossible to further increase the operating temperature. Thus, it is urgently needed to develop new materials that can withstand higher operating temperatures to achieve better performance, higher engine efficiency, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

Among various potential candidates, such as ceramics, [3] intermetallic compounds, [6] and refractory metals, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [8] have drawn considerable attention in the past decade because of their very encouraging properties, for instance, high melting points, superior mechanical properties at both room temperature and elevated temperatures, [13] which makes RHEAs of great interest for high-temperature application. The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications.
